title: Socket write-batching and pacer interaction — field notes
content:
Summary:

Short: client-side socket write coalescing (deliberate and incidental) interacts with the pacer/backpressure logic in proxies and edge queues to create multi-modal tail latency in small-request workloads. We ran a set of controlled experiments to isolate how batching at the application socket layer + pacer timers + intermediary buffering produces 3 characteristic latency modes and a couple of actionable mitigations.

Why we care:
- Many inference requests are small (prompt only or short prompts + few tokens). For these, end-to-end latency is dominated by network/transport timing, not token generation.
- Recent customer reports (low-QPS bursty traffic) show 95/99th percentile spikes that aren't explained by server-side queueing. Suspected client-proxy interaction.

Goal of this doc:
- Capture experiment setup and raw observations.
- Form hypotheses for root cause of the three latency modes.
- Propose short-term mitigations and what to instrument next.

Experiment overview:
- Date: 2026-06-18 to 2026-06-22.
- Topology: client -> remote edge proxy (envoy) -> server ingress (nginx-ish) -> inference runtime.
- Network: colocated in same AZ; baseline RTT ~1.2ms (no wifi variability). TLS everywhere (client endpoint uses HTTPS).
- Clients: 20 clients (custom Go harness) issuing synthetic predict calls. Each call: POST /v1/predict, body size ~420 bytes, expect streaming response but we measured earliest server Write() that contains initial chunk.
- Pacer: we have two pacing components in the path: the client-side pacer in runtime HTTP client (aggressive coalesce window default 150us) and the proxy egress pacer (envoy token-bucket plus fixed pacing timer 200us).
- Variants tested: (A) client coalesce window: 0, 50us, 150us, 500us; (B) proxy pacer enabled/disabled; (C) TLS record size forced via client (small vs large write calls).

Measurement method:
- Instrumented timestamps: client send-start, client socket write-complete, proxy receive, proxy forward, server write-first-byte, server sent-last, client-first-byte-received.
- Traces correlated by request-id header.
- Primary metrics: total E2E latency, time spent in client-side write-to-socket, proxy enqueue time, proxy pacer wait, server-side time-to-first-write.
- Measurement noise reduced by running in isolated cluster and repeating each variant for 10k requests.

Key observations (summary):
1) Three latency modes repeatedly appear in histograms: 
   - Mode 1 (fast): median ~8ms, E2E mostly server processing + RTT.
   - Mode 2 (mid): ~18–25ms; extra 8–12ms due to client-side coalescing window (observable when client coalesce >=150us) combined with TLS record flush timing.
   - Mode 3 (tail): 80–220ms spikes tied to proxy pacer alignment: client writes fall just after a proxy pacing window opened and then wait until next pacer tick. This produces quantized latency buckets (approx multiples of the proxy pacer tick).

2) Disabling proxy pacer collapses Mode 3 but shifts some mass into Mode 2 (proxy CPU more variable).

3) Increasing client coalesce from 50us -> 500us shifts mass from Mode 1 into Mode 2 linearly, but at 500us we also see occasional constructive alignment with proxy pacer producing Mode 3 spikes.

4) TLS record sizing: when client emits a single small write per request, TLS implementation tends to coalesce into one record; but when client performs 2 small writes with a small gap (100–200us) the TLS stack can bundle or create a second record depending on platform. That variation changes whether proxy pacer sees 1 or 2 enqueued frames, which interacts with its scheduling.

Representative numbers (from one run, 10k requests):
- Variant: client-coalesce=150us, proxy-pacer=enabled
  - p50: 9.6ms
  - p95: 23.2ms
  - p99: 132.1ms
  - tail count (>100ms): 274 (2.7%)
  - proxy-pacer-wait median: 0.2ms, p95: 120ms (aligned with tail)

Hypotheses / causal model:
- Hypothesis A: When the client coalesce window allows a write to be delayed, the proxy receives the TLS record at a different phase of its own pacing tick and misses one pacer opportunity; the request then waits for next tick -> quantized additional delay equal to pacer tick boundary.
- Hypothesis B: If multiple small TLS records for closely spaced requests arrive into a proxy queue, the proxy's batching/pacer tries to aggregate them but can be triggered by a heavy request that steals the next tick; subsequent small ones wait, producing a sawtooth of delays.
- Hypothesis C: Congestion control at TLS/TCP combined with Nagle-like behavior in client runtime induces occasional microbursts that perturb the proxy scheduler.

Short-term mitigations tried and results:
- Decrease client coalesce window to 0–50us: reduces Mode 2 mass, reduces p95 but increases number of socket syscalls (CPU tradeoff). Suitable as a short-term per-customer knob.
- Move pacer from fixed-tick (200us) to adaptive token-bucket smoothing: reduced extreme spikes by ~60% in tail but slightly increased average latency.
- Enable proxy bypass for known low-QPS customers (routing change): eliminated proxy-induced quantization but is operationally heavy.
- Server-side early flush (server calls Flush after headers): helped reduce window-sensitive variance for streaming responses by ensuring client receives first chunk earlier and doesn't wait for a larger aggregated record.

Operational recommendations:
1) Add metric: proxy-pacer-wait per-request (trace annotation) and sample at 10% to correlate with client coalesce setting.
2) Expose client-side coalesce window as runtime flag for Dedicated/Private customers with guidance (default 150us for CPU efficiency; reduce to 0–50us for latency-critical low-QPS workloads).
3) Move envoy pacer to adaptive smoothing mode in canary and measure tail reduction vs CPU overhead.
4) Document best-practice: for short-response streaming, server should do explicit small flushes to create predictable TLS record boundaries.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How much of this effect appears at global scale (cross-AZ, higher RTTs)? We expect pacer quantization to be relatively less visible when RTT >> pacer tick, but alignment effects could still produce stepped latencies in proxy local queues.
- Would a client-side small write + immediate shutdown (FIN) pattern avoid pacer alignment? This is dangerous (many sockets) and needs experiment.
- Can we reduce probe/telemetry overhead and get reliable sampling of pacer waits in production without excessive cardinality?

Next experiments planned:
- Run same sweep with RTT=10ms and RTT=50ms to test whether pacer quantization persists.
- Test real-world SDKs (python/node) to capture differences in TLS stack coalescing behavior.
- Run with QUIC (where record boundaries behave differently) to see if Mode 3 still exists.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Upload harness (client side) to PR#812 and attach run logs to JIRA-1402.
- Add envoy configuration snippet used in experiments to the confluence page.
- Pair with SDK team (Liam) to confirm default coalesce window rationale and how to expose knob safely.

Appendix (commands/config snippets):
- client flags used: --coalesce-us=150 --burst=1 --concurrency=20 --tls-min-record=256
- envoy pacer config (simplified): 
  - token_bucket: capacity 64, refill_rate 1000req/s
  - pacing_tick_us: 200 (canary-> adaptive mode)

Raw trace example (single request, timestamps ms from client start):
- client: 0.000 write-sched
- client: 0.160 write-emit (coalesce delay)
- proxy: 0.200 receive
- proxy: 0.200 queued
- proxy: 200.250 forwarded (pacer tick aligned)
- server: 200.300 first-write
- client-first-byte: 200.320

If anything in this doc looks wrong or you have other hypotheses (esp. about TLS implementation differences), please add notes or drop into #serving-runtime.

— Priya
